text: Owen had rehearsed the presentation in the shower, in the car, and twice in the bathroom mirror of his hotel, and still his hands felt like they belonged to someone else as he waited to be called into the boardroom. The panel was the same group that had turned down his last two grant proposals. He was nervous in a way he had not been since his thesis defense, the kind of anxious that made him check his phone for messages that weren't there. Beside him a junior analyst was tapping a pen against a legal pad in a fast, unconscious rhythm. Owen wondered whether he looked as jittery. He had a cup of water he kept not drinking. His daughter had texted that morning: good luck dad, dont be weird. He had written back that he would try. The door opened, and a woman with reading glasses on a chain said his name in the flat voice of someone running late. He stood, buttoned his jacket, and walked in, aware with every step that the slide clicker in his pocket was about to matter more than anything else in the room.

Title: First day managing people tomorrow and I'm so nervous I feel sick

I got promoted to team lead after four years as an individual contributor. Six people report to me now, two of whom applied for the role and didn't get it. I've been reading management books for a month, and the advice sounds sensible at 11pm and useless at 3am.

My main worry is freezing in the first one-on-one. I'm an introvert and I've never had to give hard feedback. There's one guy, Dev, who has been unhappy since the reorg, and I'm anxious about what he'll say. My manager says I'll be fine and should just listen. Easy to say.

Has anyone made the switch from peer to manager on a team where people knew you first? How did you handle the first week? Did you tell people you were nervous? Part of me thinks being honest would help, and part of me thinks it would look weak. I'd really appreciate practical advice, because right now my stomach is in knots and I keep rewriting my opening sentence.

Hey Priya,

Thanks for agreeing to look over my draft before the conference talk. I'm nervous about it, more than I expected to be. I've given talks before, but this one is in front of the people whose work I've been citing for years, and I keep worrying the central argument will sound naive to them. My hands get clammy just thinking about the Q&A.

I've been trying to be practical. I cut the slides down to twelve, wrote out the first two minutes word for word so I'd have something to hold onto, and I've been practising in the car, which my partner says is a bad habit. Still, the anxiety creeps in at night. Last Thursday I woke at four going over the one figure I'm not sure about.

If you have time this week, could you be brutal about the second section? I'd rather hear it from you now than from a stranger with a microphone. And if you think I'm overthinking everything, you're allowed to say so.

Thanks a million,
Jonah

March 4. Printed the slides at the library because the office printer jams on glossy paper. Read the agenda three times. Wore the navy blazer, then changed into the gray one, then back again. Ate half a banana standing in the hallway. The morning session ran long, so I stood at the back and listened to the speaker before me, rehearsing my first line under my breath. Phone on silent, then on again in case the hotel called. Checked my tie in the reflection of the lift doors, twice. The room has forty-two chairs, and the organizers moved me from the side slot to the main one at 10:15 this morning. Asked the AV man to test the clicker. It worked. Asked him again. Sat in the front row during the keynote and wrote the first line of my opening on the back of the program, then crossed it out. Coffee tasted like nothing. Hands dry now. My name on the screen behind the podium, spelled correctly. Stood up when the chair introduced me and felt my knees hold.

The interview room at the immigration office had a clock with no second hand, which Samir found harder to bear than he expected. He kept his documents in a folder on his knees, squared at the corners, and rechecked the dates on the marriage certificate while the officer typed. The officer asked the same question twice, in slightly different words, and Samir answered both times with the same sentence about where the couple had met. His wife sat beside him with her hands folded so tightly her knuckles had gone pale. Under the table his left foot would not stop moving. He had practiced the answers in the car, then on the bus, then in the bathroom mirror at home, but none of that prepared him for the silence after each answer, the sound of a printer warming up in the next office, the officer's pen hovering over a line before moving on. When she finally asked whether they had any photographs from the wedding, Samir reached for the envelope and found his fingers were not quite steady enough to open it.
